records.sourceFile: Nordic hamstring exercise training induces improved lower-limb swing phase mechanics and sustained strength preservation in sprinters.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Single-group longitudinal study with repeated measures in 12 male regional-to-national class sprinters (mean age 21.3 years). A standardized 4-week high-intensity Nordic Hamstring Exercise block (6 assisted and 6 unassisted sessions, compliance 92-100%) raised camera-based isokinetic peak eccentric hamstring moment at 150 deg/s by 15.5% (d = 1.14) and sprint velocity by 1.4% (d = 0.26), with most swing-phase kinematic and kinetic changes small. Hamstring function (+6% to +14%) and thigh muscle balance (+8% to +10%) remained significantly above baseline at the 3-month retention test.
records.limitations: The design has no control group, so usual sprint and resistance training, learning effects and the repeated-bout effect cannot be separated from the NHE effect. With 12 participants of mixed training history, the correlations between percentage changes are imprecise and do not show causation.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read the swing-phase correlations as evidence that NHE training makes sprinters faster, but the sprint velocity change was small and its association with the isokinetic changes was not significant (P = .306 in Table 2).

changes: paper.citation: placeholder volume and pages '2021;00:1-13' removed (header prints 'Scand J Med Sci Sports. 2021;00:1-13').
paper.findings: 'Changes in isokinetic measures' narrowed to gains in peak eccentric hamstring moment, the parameter with r = .909 and .849 in Table 2.

records.sourceFile: Overreaching and overtraining in strength sports and resistance training A scoping review.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Scoping review of 47 studies on overreaching (OR) and overtraining syndrome (OTS) in strength sports and resistance training, found by searching SPORTDiscus, Scopus and Web of Science in June 2019 (1170 records). Forty (85.1%) were observation or intervention studies, with 1 to 28 participants in the strength-sport theme and 1 to 43 in the resistance-training theme, plus 6 reviews and 1 post-hoc analysis. The authors report that short-term high-volume or high-intensity training can produce functional overreaching, that chronic high loads can produce non-functional overreaching, and that there is minimal evidence of true OTS.
records.limitations: The review maps a heterogeneous literature of small studies and does not pool effects. Most strength-sport evidence comes from weightlifters, and no powerlifting, strongman or sprinting studies were included in the strength-sport theme.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read planned overreaching as a safe, controlled stimulus, when the review states that no current test identifies the point at which functional overreaching becomes non-functional.

changes: populations: added Professional / Elite, Youth / Adolescent and Adult / Recreational (elite and junior weightlifters plus recreationally trained men in Tables 1 and 2)

evidenceSummary: '1 to 43 participants' for all studies -> 1 to 28 (theme A) and 1 to 43 (theme B), and noted 6 reviews and 1 post-hoc analysis ('Participant cohort sizes ranged from 1 to 28 in theme A and 1-43 in theme B')
paper.findings: added the throwing study, the 2 to 8 week resumption after 10 x 1-RM and the authors' note that the protocol is 'unlikely to reflect RT practice'
paper.limitations: 'does not give a formal quality appraisal' -> 'no risk-of-bias appraisal is described'; added single-author concentration (23.5%)
paper.practicalImplications: 'Coaches can use short-term planned overreaching ... to produce FOR' -> described as common practice that 'often leads to FOR' without a known transition threshold

records.sourceFile: Overtraining in Resistance   Exercise- An Exploratory Systematic Review and Methodological Appraisal of   the Literature.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Systematic review of 22 studies (14 RCTs, 2 non-randomised controlled trials, 6 uncontrolled trials) that tried to induce overreaching or overtraining through resistance exercise in healthy participants. Searches of PubMed, Web of Science and SPORTDiscus ran from inception to June 2019. Twelve studies reported a performance decline, 8 of which included follow-up performance testing, and 10 reported no decline.
records.limitations: Only 8 of the 22 studies combined a performance decline with follow-up testing, so FOR, NFOR or OTS could not be confirmed in most of the evidence. The authors could not perform a meta-analysis because methods and outcomes were heterogeneous, and most included studies came from one research group.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read the included overload protocols as validated routes to overtraining, when the authors state that few studies established overreaching or overtraining and that no biomarker other than a sustained performance decrease has been validated.

changes: populations: removed Healthy Athletes, Male Athletes and Female Athletes -> Mixed / Unspecified, Adult / Recreational; most included samples are resistance-trained or recreationally trained men, not athletes (Table 1)

paper.findings: 'Recovery times ... ranged from days to 8 weeks' -> listed reported return times by study and stated the Margonis conflict as printed (Table 2: '1RM strength returned to baseline values following 3 weeks of recovery'; Discussion: 'not restored following a 6-week taper period. These results suggest that athletes developed the OTS')
paper.rtp: 'Recovery times ... ranged from 2 days to 8 weeks' -> 'Follow-up periods ranged from 2 days to 8 weeks' (performance was 'not restored to baseline values following 2 days rest')
verification.residualConcerns: Margonis et al. time course is printed two ways (3 weeks to baseline in Table 2; not restored after a 6-week taper in the Discussion); the original study should be checked before citing it as an OTS case. The text also says nine studies without performance decline appear in Table S4 although ten are listed in Fig. 2. Volume and pages are not printed.

records.sourceFile: Parametric modeling and analysis of NFL run plays.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Statistical modeling study using NFL play-by-play data from the 2017 and 2018 regular seasons, filtered to 19,881 run plays. The authors fit a skew-t mixture model of yards gained by down, distance and line of scrimmage, with team adjustments, and print correlations of -0.432 and -0.515 between the team variance and skewness parameters and team yards per carry (p = 0.0135 and 0.00257). In a matched-pairs analysis of 2,628 pairs, outside runs gained 0.503 more yards on average (95% CI 0.160 to 0.846).
records.limitations: Team- and play-level outcomes from two NFL regular seasons, with no athlete-level physical, health or injury data. The inside/outside label comes from an external run-gap field rather than the play scheme, the matched-pairs result is observational, and the source is an uncorrected author proof.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read the outside-run yardage gain as a causal coaching lever for their own offense, when it comes from observational NFL data and labels that do not capture the play scheme.

changes: paper.methods: data source given as nflfastR -> nflscrapR for the play-by-play data, nflfastR only for run-gap labels ('obtained via the nflscrapR package')

paper.limitations: 'direction needs checking against the source' -> reports the printed negative correlations and states the conflict with the text, Fig. 8 caption and positive EPA correlations without reinterpreting ('correlations of -0.432 and -0.515 respectively')

evidenceSummary/findings: worded as printed correlations with p values; added author-proof status to identityCheck and screeningLimitations ('Journal of Sports Analytics xx (20xx) x-xx', 'Uncorrected Author Proof')
audiences: removed Performance (team play-calling model with no athlete physical outcomes)
verification.residualConcerns: Eligibility is borderline: this is a team-level play-calling statistical model with no athlete health or physical performance data. It is kept INCLUDE because it is sport-relevant original research and exclusion (c) does not apply, but a reviewer may judge it out of scope for an athlete health and performance library. Correlation sign conflict (-0.432/-0.515 printed vs positive interpretation) should not be resolved without the final published version. Volume, issue and pages are not printed (proof).

records.sourceFile: Periodization for success—In-season external training loads relative to competition load in American football.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Observational study of 27 NCAA Division II American football players whose GPS training load was recorded in 32 in-season practices and 11 games. Practices four and three days before games (GD-4, GD-3) had higher duration, distance and 2D and 3D load than games, the practice two days before (GD-2) had shorter duration than games but similar distance, and yards per minute was higher on every practice day than in games.
records.limitations: One team of 27 players, with only three linemen, limits the position and starter comparisons. The reported statistics contain inconsistencies (error df of 1,562, position groups summing to 26, abstract figures that differ from the results), so the significance results cannot be taken at face value.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read the practice and game differences as a tested periodization model that prepares players for game demands, when the study only describes loads and does not test whether any periodization approach improves performance or reduces injury.

paper.limitations: added position-group sum of 26 (Linemen n=3, Big skill n=9, Skill n=14) vs 27 participants; abstract yards-per-minute range '+15% to -11%' vs results '+15% to +11%'; kept error df and GD-1 conflict, reported as printed ('Game day minus one ... GPS units were not worn' vs abstract 'GD-4 to GD-1')
screeningLimitations: updated to cover the full set of statistical inconsistencies
paper.abstract, paper.tldr: 'practices 2 to 4 days before games' higher -> GD-4 and GD-3 higher; GD-2 shorter
paper.practicalImplications: removed 'loads set by group rather than team-wide' as untested prescription
verification.residualConcerns: Statistical reporting is internally inconsistent (error df 1,562; group sizes sum to 26; abstract GD-1 and yards-per-minute sign conflict with methods and results).
